detail.longDescription: Cython has a built-in lock, called cython.pymutex . This lock is implemented using PyThread_type_lock() in Python 3.12, and PyMutex in Python 3.13+. The Cython documentation warns against acquiring the GIL while holding a pymutex . acquire will avoid deadlocks if the GIL is held (only relevant in non-freethreading versions of Python). However, you are at risk of deadlock if you attempt to acquire the GIL while holding a cython.pymutex lock. Be aware that it is also possible for Cython to acquire the GIL implicitly (for example by raising an exception) and this is also a deadlock risk. I read this to mean that you are safe from deadlocks if you either mark your function nogil and noexcept , or acquire the GIL before you enter a pymutex locked section. But there is a third case: it is verboten to acquire the pymutex , then acquire the GIL, as this creates a risk of deadlocks. I can see a problem if there were two lock orderings: Acquire pymutex A, then acquire GIL. Acquire GIL, then acquire pymutex A. This seems like it would deadlock. But it actually doesn't: the code for #2 will repeatedly release the GIL, re-try the lock, and re-aquire the GIL . So it will never wait forever for the pymutex without releasing the GIL, so there is no lock ordering cycle in the lock ordering graph. I believe this is what the documentation is referring to in the passage, when it says that " acquire will avoid deadlocks if the GIL is held." It seems that because the Cython developers have defused lock ordering #2, they have also defused lock ordering #1. But the Cython developers do not think so. In the PR adding the warning above, they say: Acquiring a lock while holding the GIL shouldn't be able to deadlock (although the inverse isn't true). Source . However, I have not been able to construct an example of a Cython program which deadlocks as a result of acquiring the GIL inside a pymutex locked section, despite many attempts across Python 3.10-3.13, with and without freethreading. Here is one such attempt: # Cython file, named funcs.pyx cimport cython cdef cython.pymutex l # incrementing this Python int requires holding the GIL # on non ft builds of Python python_interaction = 0 def gil_in_lock(): _gil_in_lock() cdef int _gil_in_lock() noexcept nogil: global python_interaction # Take l, then take gil. with nogil: with l: with gil: python_interaction += 1 return 0 def lock_in_gil(): global python_interaction # We begin with the gil (function is not marked nogil) # Then we take l. with l: python_interaction += 1 # Python driver for funcs.pyx import threading from funcs import gil_in_lock, lock_in_gil N = 1000000 def run(fn): for _ in range(N): fn() threads = [threading.Thread(target=run, args=(f,)) for f in ([gil_in_lock] * 2 + [lock_in_gil] * 2)] for t in threads: t.start() for t in threads: t.join() print("Success! no deadlock") Is it impossible to deadlock Python in the manner the documentation warns against? If so, why? If not, can you give an example of a program that deadlocks?
